analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators order natural gas companies to refund overcharges to customers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on January 30, 2020 and died there when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the Natural Gas Act so that when the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) opens a case to investigate a natural gas company's rates, it must set a 'refund effective date' — a firm date marking when any overcharges begin to count. If FERC later finds the rates were unjust or unreasonable, it can order the company to repay customers the difference, with interest [S3]. Under current law, refunds are harder to win because there is no fixed date from which they run, so customers can pay excessive rates for long stretches with no way to get the money back [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that buy natural gas at FERC-regulated rates. If FERC finds a company charged more than a 'just and reasonable' rate, customers would get refunds with interest, covering the period from the refund effective date — set no more than five months after the case begins — through fifteen months after it, with longer refund coverage if the company stalls the case [S3].

how_it_helps.text: FERC would have to fix a refund effective date — no later than five months after a complaint is filed — so customers know the clock on their refunds has started.

FERC could order refunds, with interest, of amounts customers paid above the just and reasonable rate for the fifteen months after that date, and longer if the gas company's stalling was the main reason the case ran late.
Cases would get expedited treatment, and if FERC fails to decide within 180 days it must explain why and say when it expects to decide.

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas companies — pipeline sellers and transporters charging FERC-regulated rates — would bear the cost of paying back overcharges with interest if FERC finds their rates excessive, a cost that could fall partly on their shareholders.

drawbacks.text: Refunds are capped: customers could recover only amounts paid during the fifteen months following the refund effective date, so overcharges outside that window would be lost unless FERC finds the company deliberately stalled the case.
Companies subject to refund liability would face added regulatory and financial risk, which pipeline companies argue could raise financing costs and eventually push rates up for consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For customers who overpaid, the bill offers a real remedy where today the excess can go unrecovered because no refund date is fixed. The fifteen-month cap means the remedy is partial, and companies' claims that refund liability could raise future rates deserve to be taken seriously — though the bill does require FERC to prove rates were unjust, so the burden stays on regulators and complainants rather than on companies by default.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 30, 2020 by Rep. G. K. Butterfield with Rep. Billy Long as the bill's one cosponsor, a Republican.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas companies are better off: without the bill, no fixed refund date exists, so customers who paid FERC-regulated rates later found excessive have a harder path to getting that money back.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Natural gas companies facing refund claims

for.name: Rep. Billy Long
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it remained in committee until the 116th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two House sponsors were a Democrat and a Republican, but with no hearing, vote, or recorded opposition, the record shows too little to say how support or opposition split by party.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline companies (FERC-regulated sellers and transporters)
industries.note: The bill would expose them to orders to refund, with interest, amounts charged above FERC-approved 'just and reasonable' rates. That liability is exactly what customers lack a reliable remedy for under current law.

industries.industry: Residential and commercial natural gas customers
industries.note: Customers who paid excessive rates would recover the difference with interest for a defined window, converting regulatory findings into actual money back.
